messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Error in dsm
messages.body_plain:
This seems like odd behaviour and not something I've seen before.

I was unable to reproduce the issue on my machine using the example
dolphins data.

A couple of follow-up questions that might aid the diagnosis:

1) Does the error definitely occur after the print(p) an not before?
2) If "yes" above: it's possible that your gg.opts includes something
unusual, perhaps incompatible with what dsm gives you. If you can paste
what gg.opts is perhaps we can see what the offending code is?
3) If "no" to 1): Are you using up-to-date R and packages (you can
ensure you have the most recent versions from CRAN using
update.packages()). If that doesn't work, if you can send (direct to me
rather than the Google Group your data and code that reproduces the
error I can take a look.

best,
--dave

messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] qq plots
messages.body_plain:
This message is produced by Distance to prevent the QQ-plot from becoming over-crowded; it is not an error message.  All observations will be included in the calculation of the goodness of fit tests, just not all points will be shown on the QQ-plot  The maximum number of points on the QQ-plot can be adjusted in the "Diagnostics" button in the "Detection function" tab in the CDS and MCDS analysis engine.  The analysis engine can be accessed from the "Model Definition Properties".

See the screen capture I provide along with this email.

messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] preddata with ArcGis
messages.body_plain:
Hi Julia, listfolk,

The question of how large to make the prediction grid cells is common in
DSM methodology and I don't have a complete answer (others should
obviously chime in if they have other thoughts...) My feeling is this
probably heavily depends on the animals your studying and the area in
which you study them.

Two general thoughts:

I think the main issue to be aware of is the resolution of the grid on
which your covariates live: it's possible in Arc and other packages to
interpolate to fine scales -- this may not be advisable (depending on
your covariates. So, sticking to scales similar to those that the data
were collected on seems sensible. Conversely, going much bigger may
average out interesting or troublesome patterns in the covariates, which
you may view as negative or positive. (Recent work of Foster et al 2012
and Stoklosa et al 2015 highlight this kind of issue, though don't
directly address what we're talking about here.)

Secondly, sticking on a scale the size of the segments in your data or
larger also seems prudent, as the model doesn't know more about the
distribution of the animals in question than at the scale of the segments.

My plan is to run some simulations to check my thoughts above in the
near future, should I get around to that I will post to this list as
there has been previous interest in this topic.

If anyone else has experience or has seen relevant literature on this
topic, please do post this here!

Hope this helps!
--dave

References:

Foster, S.D., Shimadzu, H. & Darnell, R. (2012) Uncertainty in spatially
predicted covariates: is it ignorable? Journal of the Royal Statistical
Society, Series C, 61, 637–652.

Stoklosa, J., Daly, C., Foster, S. D., Ashcroft, M. B., Warton, D. I.
(2015), A climate of uncertainty: accounting for error in climate
variables for species distribution models. Methods in Ecology and
Evolution, 6: 412–423. doi: 10.1111/2041-210X.12217

messages.subject: Re: Mulitple helicopters cause detection function woes
messages.subject_clean: Mulitple helicopters cause detection function woes
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I wanted to post about what I decided to do with the above data in case it is helpful to others.

Based on some feedback from Eric, it seems the histograms weren't as poorly behaved as I had though.

The key point was deciding if we had an issue with g(0)<1, as if not, then based on the property of pooling robustness, we could ignore variability in detectability by aircraft type, as we were just going for a density estimate for the whole survey (aircraft isn't really an interesting covariate, as sex or species might be).

We did decide to assume g(0)=1 after discussing more with the biologists regarding the visibility issues in the EC-120 in particular. It seems like the vision of the front observer (who is responsible for the area under the helicopter) was reduced only on the right from about 30-100 m from the line. Given that transects are not all flown in the same direction, and that the height of the aircraft varies during the survey, we decided that although some of the animals may have been missed in that region, visibiilty of the line itself (<30m) was good, and the g(0)=1 assumption was probably no more compromised than in a usual survey (due to canopy cover).

After right-truncation and selecting the best model (half-normal + cosine), I did try that model and include aircraft as a covariate. It was not supported by AIC, and so our final estimate is based on the half-normal + cosine.

I should also add that I was sorely tempted to try left-truncation to remove what I perceived as a hole at 0, but was saved from that by Eric's reminder that the final density estimate will likely be very sensitive to you choice of left-truncation distance, and in the absence of any independant information about the appropriate truncation distance, this is likely not a wise approach.

Hannah

            convert.units = 1, family = quasipoisson(link = "log"), group = TRUE,
            gamma = 1.4, control = list(keepData = TRUE), availability = 1,

I compared my dataset with the dolphins data to make sure that all my columns were defined correctly as factors, numerical or integrer and that I had all the required ones. I don't understand why the error message is talking about cluster.name <http://cluster.name> because I have no column with that name and it's not a prerequisite according to the package instruction.

All help would be greatly appreciated and I'd be very grateful because I am totally blocked by this error.

Thanks,
Julia

messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Error in DSM
messages.body_plain:
Julia:

Regarding the "cluster.name <http://cluster.name>" error; by setting the argument "group=TRUE" you are estimating abundance/density of groups in your population, rather than abundance/density of individuals.  This is an unusual situation.  The dsm() functions presumes the existence of a field named "size" to indicate the size of each group detected.  I expect the absence of a field named "size" is what caused the error.

Regarding your previous question on area of prediction grid cells--for our demonstration (spotted dolphin) dsm project, we've used the ETOPO2v2 NOAA database.  With that database open in ArcGIS, you can examine the "area" property of the grid cells to determine prediction grid cell size for use with this bathymetry data.

messages.subject: Third notice: distance sampling workshops, August 2015, St. Andrews
messages.subject_clean: Third notice: distance sampling workshops, August 2015, St. Andrews
messages.body_plain:
The Centre for Research into Ecological and Environmental Modelling (CREEM) is hosting two linked workshops in the summer of 2015 in our purpose-built facilities at the University of St. Andrews, Scotland. The aim of these workshops is to train participants in the latest methods for design and analysis of distance sampling surveys, including line and point transects. The workshops are taught by leading researchers in the field, using industry-standard software.  We will be using the latest version of Distance, Version 7, currently in test release, available here: http://distancesampling.org/Distance/distance70download.html

The first workshop (11-14 August) will run at an introductory level, and will focus on distance sampling methods, largely described in the standard reference book "Introduction to Distance Sampling." The workshop will be a blend of theory and practice and participants will learn how to use the program "Distance." Participants will gain a solid grounding in both survey design and methods of analysis for distance sampling surveys.  'Automated survey design' and 'incorporating covariates in detection function' have moved from the advanced workshop into the introductory workshop.

The advanced distance sampling workshop (17-20 August) will include advanced treatment of:  analyses in which detectability on the transect line is not assumed to be perfect (the so-called g(0) problem) and spatial (or  density surface) modelling. We will showcase a series of new R packages we have developed for performing standard as well as sophisticated analyses in R. The aim of this workshop is to bring participants up to date with the latest developments in distance sampling methods and software. It is also an opportunity for those actively engaged in the design, analysis and execution of distance sampling surveys to discuss common issues and problems, and set future research directions. The workshop will be a combination of lectures and computer sessions, with considerable time for discussion.

For all workshops, participants are encouraged to bring their own data sets, and can expect to do some preliminary analyses with their data.  Computer sessions take place in our computer classroom (attached to the seminar room); participants can use our computers or bring their own laptops.

 Additional details regarding the workshop can be found at our website
http://creem2.st-andrews.ac.uk/workshops/distance-sampling-workshops-st-andrews-august-2015/
--
Eric Rexstad
Research Unit for Wildlife Population Assessment
Centre for Research into Ecological and Environmental Modelling
University of St. Andrews
St. Andrews Scotland KY16 9LZ
